turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, this screen just froze on me again. Okay, Mr. Hale, what brings you in?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): The cough, mostly in the morning. And I get winded just walking out to the mailbox. Parking was a mess, but that's not why I'm here.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has the cough been going on?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Months? Maybe longer. It's worst right when I get up.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hold on, the chart just jumped. Say that timing again?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): A few months at least. I can't pin the start down.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any phlegm with it, or is it dry?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Mornings there's some gunk. It was yellow for a bit after that chest thing, but now it's mostly clear, I think.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): The chest thing, when was that?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): About three weeks ago. Urgent care told me it was a chest infection and handed me antibiotics.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which antibiotic? I'm not seeing it on here.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, the pink pills. Azithromycin, I think. Five days, and I finished the pack.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the cough, did that clear after the pills?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): The heavy part eased off. The morning cough is still there, though, and so is getting winded.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is the breathlessness new, or has it been around?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, it's been creeping up. Stairs are the worst. I have to stop halfway up.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain with that?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about fever or night sweats?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Not now. I had a fever with the infection, but that's gone. No night sweats.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you wheeze?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Sometimes, yeah, in the morning. I don't know if you'd call it wheezing. More like a little whistle.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): About ten a day. Well, actually, maybe twenty. Depends on the day. I've smoked since I was a teenager, so, what, forty years?
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, something just pinged. Was that ten or twenty?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Closer to twenty, I guess. I don't know, doctor. I don't really count them.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any inhalers?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): The rescue one, albuterol. Two puffs when I need it. And they gave me fluticasone, but I don't use that one much.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): How often for each? Sorry, say it once more, I clicked the wrong tab.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Albuterol, some days twice, some days not at all. The steroid one I forget. Maybe a few times a week if I remember, and I don't know the dose.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me pull up this morning's spirometry. One second. FEV1 is one point seven two liters, 61 percent predicted. FVC is 3.05 liters, and the ratio is 56 percent.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that bad? Last time, a couple years back, they said it was borderline. I don't know what the numbers were.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Say that again? Borderline when?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Maybe two years ago, at the other clinic. They just said borderline and to cut back on smoking. I didn't.

[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Looking at today's numbers, this is an obstructive pattern. I'm thinking COPD, with the smoking and that morning cough. It could still be leftover from the infection, though. I don't want to lock that in today.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): So do I need more medicine, or what?

[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): I want you using the fluticasone, two puffs twice a day, every day, not just when you remember. Albuterol stays two puffs when you're short of breath, up to every four hours.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay, I'll try. The quitting thing, I don't know, doctor. I've said I would a hundred times.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll refer you to the smoking cessation clinic. They can go over patches or whatever fits. And I'm ordering a chest x-ray to be sure that infection cleared.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Do I gotta come back for all this?
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back in three months. If the breathing gets worse before then, come in sooner.

omissions.text: Exertional breathlessness requires him to stop halfway up the stairs.

Patient reported he does not know the fluticasone dose before today's instruction; prior use was only 'a few times a week if I remember.' Recording fluticasone simply as currently used at 2 puffs twice a day misses that this is a new instructed regimen rather than the prior actual usage.
Azithromycin course was for a chest infection diagnosed at urgent care about three weeks ago, and he finished the pack.
